metadata.title: Green at Fifteen? How 15-year-olds perform in environmental science and geoscience in PISA 2006

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This report uses PISA 2006 microdata covering 15-year-olds in 57 countries/economies, with nationally representative samples drawn for the PISA assessment. For school-level questionnaire responses, the report states that principals’ responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school. For student-level results, the report describes OECD/PISA reporting conventions (e.g., OECD averages as arithmetic means of country estimates) but does not specify the exact student weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures in the provided text. Because this is an OECD/PISA analytical report rather than an ML modeling paper, the appropriate weighting approach is the PISA complex survey design used in the underlying PISA database; however, the manuscript excerpt does not document the specific weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate methods.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This report is primarily a descriptive and correlational analysis of PISA 2006 environmental science and geoscience indices and attitudinal indices, rather than an empirical ML model that explicitly documents plausible-value (PV) combination rules. While PISA achievement is typically based on PVs, the excerpt provided does not specify PV handling (e.g., Rubin’s rules) for the constructed environmental science/geoscience indices. Missing-data handling is also not documented at the level of an explicit imputation/deletion strategy for the analytic models in the excerpt; instead, the report provides general symbols for missingness in tables and notes that some data were removed for technical reasons.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses the PISA 2006 target population of 15-year-olds (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) who have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of institution type. For the environmental science and geoscience performance indices, it constructs indices from a subset of PISA 2006 science items: 24 environment-related questions (14 geoscience-focused) out of 108 science questions, and reports proficiency levels A–D based on item response modeling. For attitudinal analyses, it uses student questionnaire items (and in some countries parent questionnaire indices are available) and notes that comparisons should be interpreted cautiously due to cross-country differences in how students answer attitudinal questions. The excerpt does not provide a detailed listwise/pairwise deletion rule; instead, it provides table symbols for missingness (e.g., category not applicable, too few observations, data not available/withdrawn) and notes that some parent indices were not estimated for Poland due to data problems.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes PISA 2006 science data with an environmental context, constructing two performance indices: an environmental science index based on 24 environment-related science items (including 14 geoscience items) and a geoscience sub-index based on the geoscience subset. Proficiency is reported at four levels (A highest to D lowest), and results are summarized using both proficiency distributions and mean country scores on a 500-point international scale (SD=100). The report also uses PISA student and parent questionnaires to build indices of responsibility, optimism, and awareness of complex environmental issues, and examines associations between these indices and environmental science performance after accounting for student and school background variables. It reports substantial cross-country variation in the share reaching Level D and Level A, with lower performance concentrated among immigrant and disadvantaged socio-economic groups. The excerpt does not document PV combination rules or a specific missing-data strategy for the constructed indices, so interpretability for model-based inference is limited to the descriptive/correlational framing used throughout.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD/PISA analytical report rather than an empirical ML paper that trains and evaluates predictive models. The excerpt provides extensive descriptive results (proficiency distributions, mean scores, and regression-based associations for attitudinal indices) but does not specify any ML algorithms, PV handling procedures, or missing-data imputation/deletion rules at the level required for ML-method extraction. Therefore, ML technique fields are left empty and main_findings are not fabricated as predictive ML outcomes.
